Howell JJ.role: Metabolism biologist who, as a postdoc in Brendan Manning's lab at Harvard, worked out how the diabetes drug metformin switches off mTORC1 in the liver, and who later moved into drug and gene-therapy research in industry
Howell JJ.sub: Lead (Principal) Scientist and Project Manager, Spark Therapeutics (per Manning lab alumni page) · scientist, Navitor Pharmaceuticals, Cambridge, Massachusetts (2019 paper) · postdoctoral fellow, Manning lab, Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health (2010–2016) · Markus Stoffel's group, Institute of Molecular Systems Biology, ETH Zurich (papers 2008–2009)
story: Metformin is the most widely prescribed diabetes drug and is also tested as a possible anti-aging medicine, yet how it acts inside cells has long been debated. In HOW2017, Jessica Howell, working in Brendan Manning's lab, asked how metformin reaches mTORC1, the growth-control complex that tells cells when to build proteins and fats. In mouse liver and in liver cells the study found that metformin lowers the cell's energy supply and that, at lower doses, this shuts down mTORC1 through two known brakes: the energy sensor AMPK and the TSC complex. At higher doses other routes come into play. The study is a direct mechanistic link between a common drug, cellular energy sensing and the mTOR pathway, though it was done in mice and cultured cells, not in people.

Howell's earlier research was on how insulin controls the liver. In Markus Stoffel's group at the Institute of Molecular Systems Biology, ETH Zurich, Howell studied the transcription factor Foxa2 and showed in 2009 that insulin turns it off by phosphorylation rather than by moving it out of the nucleus. Howell joined the Manning lab in 2010, co-wrote reviews on how mTOR links nutrient sensing to whole-body metabolism and drives the building of proteins, lipids and nucleic acids, and contributed to the finding that chronic mTORC1 activation in mouse liver is enough to cause liver cancer.

After the Manning lab Howell worked at Navitor Pharmaceuticals in Cambridge, Massachusetts, on a 2019 study that found small molecules which selectively block mTORC1 by inhibiting glucose transporters. The Manning lab alumni page lists the current position as Lead (Principal) Scientist and Project Manager at Spark Therapeutics, a gene-therapy company.

highlights.HOW2017: First author: showed in mouse liver and liver cells that metformin lowers cell energy and, at low doses, inhibits mTORC1 through AMPK and the TSC complex.

Howell JJ.note: Current position (Spark Therapeutics) comes only from the Manning lab alumni page, which is undated. ETH Zurich work with Markus Stoffel is from 2008-2009 papers; that it was her PhD is not confirmed, so the text does not call it a PhD.

Talbott G.lab_name: Manning Lab, Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health (Boston, Massachusetts, USA)
Talbott G.role: Research assistant in Brendan Manning's mTOR lab at Harvard in 2013 and 2014, who contributed to studies on where the TSC complex sits in the cell and how metformin reaches mTORC1
Talbott G.sub: Research Associate, The Jackson Laboratory (per Manning lab alumni page) · research assistant, Manning lab, Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health (2013–2014, at the time of the studies)
story: George Talbott appears in this Atlas on two papers from Brendan Manning's lab at the Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health. MEN2014 showed that the TSC complex, the main brake on mTORC1 (the growth-control complex), works by sitting on the surface of the lysosome, the cell's recycling compartment where mTORC1 is switched on. Insulin pushes the TSC complex off the lysosome, which releases the brake, so the cell can combine signals about hormones and nutrients at one place. HOW2017 showed in mouse liver and liver cells that the diabetes drug metformin lowers cell energy and, at low doses, inhibits mTORC1 through the energy sensor AMPK and the TSC complex.

The Manning lab alumni page lists Talbott as a research assistant in the lab from 2013 to 2014 and gives a later position as Research Associate at The Jackson Laboratory, a mouse genetics research institute. No other official page was found, so the present role could not be confirmed.

highlights.HOW2017: Co-author, from the time as a research assistant in the Manning lab, on the paper showing metformin inhibits mTORC1 in mouse liver through AMPK and the TSC complex.
highlights.MEN2014: Co-author on the paper showing that insulin moves the TSC complex off the lysosome, releasing the brake on mTORC1.

Talbott G.note: Later PubMed papers by a 'George C Talbott' at Verndari Inc. and California Northstate University (Sacramento area) were not linked to this person and were left out. Jackson Laboratory position is from the undated alumni page only.

Turner M.lab_name: Manning Lab, Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health (Boston, Massachusetts, USA)
Turner M.role: Research assistant and lab manager in Brendan Manning's mTOR lab at Harvard from 2014 to 2016, who contributed to studies on nucleotide synthesis in tumour cells and on metformin's route to mTORC1
Turner M.sub: Postdoctoral Fellow, University of California, San Francisco (per Manning lab alumni page) · research assistant and lab manager, Manning lab, Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health (2014–2016, at the time of the studies)
story: Marc Turner is a co-author on two Atlas papers from Brendan Manning's lab. VAL2017 studied cells that lack the TSC genes, so their mTORC1 (the growth-control complex) is always on. Such cells make DNA building blocks, nucleotides, at a high rate to keep up with growth; when nucleotide supply falls behind demand, DNA copying stalls, a condition called replication stress. The study used this imbalance as a weak point that drugs can target, tested in cells and mouse tumour models. HOW2017 showed in mouse liver and liver cells that the diabetes drug metformin lowers cell energy and, at low doses, inhibits mTORC1 through AMPK and the TSC complex.

The Manning lab alumni page lists Turner as research assistant and lab manager from 2014 to 2016 and gives a later position as Postdoctoral Fellow at the University of California, San Francisco. The common surname made it impossible to match later PubMed papers with confidence, so present research is not described here.

highlights.VAL2017: Co-author on the paper linking hyperactive mTORC1 to nucleotide demand and a drug-sensitive weakness in TSC-deficient cells.
highlights.HOW2017: Co-author on the paper showing metformin inhibits mTORC1 in mouse liver through AMPK and the TSC complex.

Turner M.note: UCSF postdoc is from the undated alumni page only; no UCSF page or PubMed record could be tied to him.

de Oliveira Isídio BE.lab_name: Laboratory of Molecular Studies and Experimental Therapy, Department of Genetics, Federal University of Pernambuco (Recife, Brazil)
de Oliveira Isídio BE.role: Researcher in Antonio Carlos de Freitas's laboratory at the Federal University of Pernambuco who studies whether human papillomavirus (HPV) is active in breast tumours
de Oliveira Isídio BE.sub: Laboratory of Molecular Studies and Experimental Therapy, Department of Genetics, Federal University of Pernambuco (papers 2024–2026, at the time of the study)
story: HPV, the virus that causes most cervical cancers, carries three cancer-promoting genes called E5, E6 and E7. A question still under debate is whether the virus also plays a part in some breast cancers. In DEOLIVEIRA2026, Beatriz Eda de Oliveira Isídio and colleagues in Recife measured these viral genes and the RNA messages of the PI3K/AKT/mTOR growth pathway in breast tumour samples. Of 92 patients, 48 had usable RNA. Tumours expressing HPV16 genes had higher PI3K and lower mTOR transcript levels. The design only shows an association between two sets of RNA measurements in tissue, so it does not prove that the virus switches the mTOR pathway on or off.

The work continues a line from the same laboratory, led by Antonio Carlos de Freitas in the Department of Genetics at the Federal University of Pernambuco. In a 2024 study of 56 patients from northeastern Brazil, on which de Oliveira Isídio was a co-author, the group detected HPV in about a third of breast tumours, mostly HPV16, often with high viral load and active E5. No institutional profile was found, so the affiliation shown is the one on the Atlas paper.

highlights.DEOLIVEIRA2026: First author: measured HPV16 E5, E6 and E7 expression and PI3K/AKT/mTOR transcripts in breast tumour samples, finding an association but not a causal link.

Sinclair DA.lab_name: Sinclair Lab, Paul F. Glenn Center for Biology of Aging Research, Department of Genetics, Harvard Medical School (Boston, Massachusetts, USA)
Sinclair DA.role: Geneticist of aging at Harvard Medical School, known for work on sirtuins, NAD+ and the idea that aging stems from a loss of epigenetic information, who appears in this Atlas as a co-author on two mouse lifespan studies
Sinclair DA.sub: Professor of Genetics, Harvard Medical School, and founding director, Paul F. Glenn Laboratories for the Biological Mechanisms of Aging · conjoint professor, School of Medical Sciences, University of New South Wales · faculty, Harvard Medical School (since 1999) · postdoc, Leonard Guarente lab, MIT · PhD in molecular genetics, University of New South Wales (1995)
story: David Sinclair is a middle author on two Atlas studies about diet, drugs and lifespan in mice. SOL2014, led by Samantha Solon-Biet and Stephen Simpson in Sydney, fed mice diets that differed in their mix of protein, carbohydrate and fat and let them eat freely. Lifespan and heart and metabolic health depended on the ratio of protein to carbohydrate, not on the total calories eaten, and mice on low-protein, high-carbohydrate diets had lower mTOR activation in the liver. STR2012, from the NIA Interventions Testing Program, tested five popular candidates, including resveratrol, green tea extract and curcumin, in genetically mixed mice. None changed lifespan significantly. The paper is a clear example of publishing negative results, which helps others avoid chasing compounds that do not work.

Sinclair earned his PhD in molecular genetics at the University of New South Wales in 1995, studying gene regulation in yeast. He then spent about four years in Leonard Guarente's lab at MIT, where yeast was used as a model of aging, and joined Harvard Medical School in 1999. His lab has worked on sirtuins, a family of enzymes that need the molecule NAD+, on mitochondria, and on partial reprogramming with Yamanaka factors to restore youthful gene activity in mouse tissues. He proposes an 'information theory of aging', in which aging comes from a gradual loss of epigenetic information, the chemical marks that tell each cell which genes to use.

He is Professor of Genetics at Harvard Medical School, founding director of the Paul F. Glenn Laboratories for the Biological Mechanisms of Aging, and a conjoint professor at the University of New South Wales. Some of his claims, including early work on resveratrol as a sirtuin activator and public statements about reversing aging, have been disputed by other researchers.

highlights.SOL2014: Co-author on the mouse study showing that the protein-to-carbohydrate ratio, not calorie intake, shaped lifespan and metabolic health, with lower liver mTOR activation on low-protein diets.
highlights.STR2012: Co-author on the Interventions Testing Program report in which none of five popular compounds, including resveratrol, extended mouse lifespan significantly.

Sinclair DA.note: Training and titles are from Wikipedia plus the Harvard lab home page; the HMS faculty profile could not be opened because the web search budget ran out. The lab name uses the Glenn Center wording; check against the HMS page. The text mentions, neutrally, that some of his claims (resveratrol, reversing aging) are disputed; remove if Petr prefers no mention.

O'Kane CJ.lab_name: O'Kane Lab, Department of Genetics, University of Cambridge (Cambridge, England, United Kingdom)
O'Kane CJ.role: Fruit-fly geneticist at Cambridge who studies how the endoplasmic reticulum is built inside nerve fibres and how its failure causes hereditary spastic paraplegia, and who helped bring Drosophila models into David Rubinsztein's autophagy work
O'Kane CJ.sub: Professor of Genetics, Department of Genetics, University of Cambridge, and Fellow of Churchill College · postdoc, University of Basel (enhancer trapping in Drosophila) · PhD in bacterial genetics, Trinity College Dublin · BA in Genetics, University of Cambridge
story: Cahir O'Kane appears on three Atlas papers from David Rubinsztein's group, where O'Kane's lab supplied fruit-fly (Drosophila) genetics. RAV2004 showed that blocking mTOR switches on autophagy, the cell's self-cleaning system, which then cleared the toxic protein clumps of Huntington's disease and improved symptoms in flies given rapamycin and in mice given the related drug CCI-779. BER2006 extended this to several other aggregate-prone proteins in cultured cells and showed that rapamycin reduced the toxicity of human tau in flies. KOR2011 found that where the lysosome sits in the cell helps decide whether mTORC1, the growth-control complex, is on: with nutrients present lysosomes move to the cell edge and mTORC1 is active, while starvation pulls them towards the nucleus, mTORC1 falls and autophagy starts.

O'Kane studied genetics as an undergraduate at Cambridge and took a PhD in bacterial genetics at Trinity College Dublin. As a postdoc at the University of Basel O'Kane helped develop enhancer trapping in Drosophila, a method for finding where and when genes are switched on in the fly. O'Kane is now Professor of Genetics in the Department of Genetics at Cambridge and a Fellow of Churchill College.

The O'Kane lab uses Drosophila to study the endoplasmic reticulum (ER), a network of membrane tubes that runs along nerve axons. The group has linked several proteins that are mutated in hereditary spastic paraplegia, an inherited disease in which the longest nerve fibres slowly degenerate, to the formation of this axonal ER, and it images the network by light and electron microscopy.

highlights.KOR2011: Co-author on the paper showing that lysosome position inside the cell tunes mTORC1 activity and autophagy.
highlights.BER2006: Co-author, providing fly genetics, on the paper showing that rapamycin reduces the toxicity of several aggregate-prone proteins in cells and of human tau in Drosophila.
highlights.RAV2004: Co-author, providing fly genetics, on the paper showing that mTOR inhibition induces autophagy and reduces Huntington's disease toxicity in fly and mouse models.

sources: PubMed search O'Kane CJ[Author] AND Drosophila AND (endoplasmic reticulum OR spastic paraplegia)
O'Kane CJ.note: Full name with middle initial 'Cahir J. O'Kane' follows PubMed initials CJ; the department page uses 'Cahir O'Kane'. The statement that his lab provided fly genetics in BER2006/RAV2004 is inferred from his field and the fly experiments; check if Petr wants it softened.

Powers RW.lab_name: Sterne, Kessler, Goldstein & Fox P.L.L.C. (Washington, DC, USA)
Powers RW.role: Molecular biologist who, as a PhD student in Seattle, built high-throughput lifespan screens in yeast and showed that lowering TOR signalling extends chronological lifespan, and who later became a patent attorney
Powers RW.sub: Associate, Litigation Group, Sterne, Kessler, Goldstein & Fox (patent law) · PhD in molecular biology, University of Washington and Fred Hutchinson Cancer Research Center (Stanley Fields lab, Department of Genome Sciences) · BA in biology, University of Virginia
story: Yeast cells age in two ways that can be measured in the lab. Replicative lifespan counts how many times a mother cell can divide; chronological lifespan measures how long cells that have stopped dividing stay alive, a rough model for non-dividing tissues in animals. In POW2006, R. Wilson Powers, working in Stanley Fields's lab at the University of Washington with Matt Kaeberlein and Brian Kennedy, built a high-throughput assay and measured chronological lifespan for about 4,800 yeast strains, each missing one gene. Several long-lived strains carried mutations in the TOR pathway, the nutrient-sensing system that mTOR belongs to in animals. Removing the amino acids asparagine or glutamate from the growth medium, or blocking TOR with rapamycin or methionine sulfoximine, also lengthened survival. The study, done only in yeast, supported the idea that lower TOR signalling is one way calorie restriction extends life.

Powers did a BA in biology at the University of Virginia and a PhD in molecular biology at the University of Washington and the Fred Hutchinson Cancer Research Center, where he developed high-throughput assays for measuring the lifespan of yeast cells. He was also a co-author of the 2005 Science paper by Kaeberlein and colleagues showing that TOR and Sch9 regulate yeast replicative lifespan in response to nutrients.

He then moved into intellectual property law. A professional profile lists him as an associate in the Litigation Group of Sterne, Kessler, Goldstein & Fox, working on patent litigation, patent drafting and freedom-to-operate opinions in the life sciences.

highlights.POW2006: First author: ran the genome-wide yeast screen showing that reduced TOR signalling extends chronological lifespan.

Powers RW.note: Current position is from a National Law Review author page, which may be dated; the firm's office city (Washington, DC) is not stated on that page and is assumed from the firm. Co-authorship of the 2005 Science paper (Kaeberlein et al., TOR and Sch9) is from a bibliographic record seen in search results.

Sun Z.lab_name: Department of Hematology, The First Affiliated Hospital of Zhejiang Chinese Medical University (Hangzhou, Zhejiang, China)
Sun Z.role: Hematology researcher in Hangzhou who studies treatment of bone-marrow failure, including the use of sirolimus (rapamycin) in pure red cell aplasia
Sun Z.sub: Department of Hematology, The First Affiliated Hospital of Zhejiang Chinese Medical University (Zhejiang Provincial Hospital of Chinese Medicine) and The First School of Clinical Medicine, Zhejiang Chinese Medical University (papers 2026)
story: In pure red cell aplasia, the bone marrow stops making red blood cells while white cells and platelets are spared. The acquired form is often driven by the immune system, so it is treated with immune-suppressing drugs such as ciclosporin. In SUN2026, Zexing Sun and colleagues in Dijiong Wu's group looked back at patients treated at one hospital whose disease had not responded to ciclosporin and who then received sirolimus, the drug also called rapamycin, which blocks mTOR in immune cells. 54.5 percent responded, and 64.3 percent of those whose aplasia was secondary to another disease. Responses did not depend on mutations in STAT3 or STAT5B, genes often altered in the abnormal lymphocytes linked to this disease. The study was retrospective, at one centre, with no randomised control group, so it cannot prove that sirolimus works better than ciclosporin.

Sun works in the Department of Hematology of the First Affiliated Hospital of Zhejiang Chinese Medical University in Hangzhou. In 2026 the same group also published a single-centre comparison of stem cell transplant donor types in aplastic anaemia, on which Sun was a co-author. No personal institutional page was found, so the affiliation shown is the one on the Atlas paper.

highlights.SUN2026: First author of the retrospective single-centre study in which second-line sirolimus produced responses in ciclosporin-refractory acquired pure red cell aplasia regardless of STAT3/STAT5B status.

Xu C.lab_name: Department of Hematology, The Seventh Affiliated Hospital, Sun Yat-sen University (Shenzhen, China)
Xu C.role: Hematologist in Shenzhen who studies drug resistance and drug safety in multiple myeloma, and senior author of a study linking a small RNA fragment to autophagy-driven resistance to bortezomib
Xu C.sub: Department of Hematology, The Seventh Affiliated Hospital, Sun Yat-sen University, Shenzhen (papers 2025–2026)
story: Multiple myeloma is a cancer of plasma cells, the antibody factories of the bone marrow. A standard drug against it is bortezomib, which blocks the proteasome, the machine that destroys unwanted proteins, so that myeloma cells choke on their own protein waste. Many patients eventually stop responding. In FU2026, Cong Xu's group found that a small RNA piece cut from a transfer RNA, called tRF-17-8SPOL52, is raised in relapsed or treatment-resistant myeloma. It lowers RUBCN, a protein that normally holds back autophagy, the cell's self-digestion system. With the brake removed, autophagy speeds up and helps myeloma cells survive bortezomib. The link to mTOR is indirect: autophagy is one of the main processes mTORC1 keeps in check.

Xu works in the Department of Hematology of the Seventh Affiliated Hospital of Sun Yat-sen University in Shenzhen. In 2025 Xu was senior author of a study that used the US FDA adverse event reporting database to map lung side effects, such as pneumonia and interstitial lung disease, linked to the antibody drugs approved for myeloma. No personal institutional page was found, so the affiliation shown is the one on the Atlas paper.

highlights.FU2026: Senior and corresponding author: led the study showing that tRF-17-8SPOL52 drives bortezomib resistance in myeloma by suppressing RUBCN and increasing autophagy.

Xu C.note: Common name: only papers with the same hospital and myeloma focus were used (two ties).

Horvath S.lab_name: Department of Human Genetics, David Geffen School of Medicine, University of California, Los Angeles (Los Angeles, California, USA)
Horvath S.role: Biostatistician and geneticist who built the first pan-tissue epigenetic clock, a DNA methylation test that estimates biological age, and co-developed the network method WGCNA
Horvath S.sub: Principal investigator, Altos Labs · Professor of Human Genetics, David Geffen School of Medicine, and of Biostatistics, Fielding School of Public Health, University of California, Los Angeles (faculty since 2000) · ScD in Biostatistics, Harvard School of Public Health (2000) · PhD in Mathematics, University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill (1995) · Diplom in Mathematics and Physics, Technische Universität Berlin (1989)
story: Cells carry chemical tags on their DNA, called methyl groups, and the pattern of these tags shifts with age in a predictable way. An epigenetic clock reads the pattern at selected sites and turns it into an age estimate. In HOR2021, Steve Horvath and colleagues, with Adam Salmon's group in San Antonio, built two such clocks for the blood of common marmosets, small short-lived monkeys used in aging research. One clock, trained on both human and marmoset data, also tracked age reasonably well in vervet monkeys and rhesus macaques. In a separate group of marmosets they asked whether rapamycin, the mTOR-blocking drug that lengthens life in mice, would make blood look younger by this measure. The clocks did not detect a significant change. This is a null result for one biomarker in blood; it does not show that rapamycin has no effect on aging in marmosets.

Horvath trained first in mathematics and physics at the Technische Universität Berlin, took a PhD in mathematics at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill in 1995 and an ScD in biostatistics at the Harvard School of Public Health in 2000. He joined UCLA that year as a professor of human genetics and of biostatistics. With members of his lab he developed weighted correlation network analysis (WGCNA), a widely used method for finding groups of genes that act together. In 2013 he published the Horvath clock, a DNA methylation age estimator that works across nearly all tissues and cell types, and he co-founded the non-profit Clock Foundation.
He is now a principal investigator at Altos Labs, a company that studies cell rejuvenation, and is still listed as a professor at UCLA.

highlights.HOR2021: First author: built marmoset epigenetic clocks for blood and found no significant effect of rapamycin on epigenetic age.

Horvath S.note: Sources are Wikipedia and PubMed only (web search budget ran out). Altos Labs site/city not confirmed, so lab_name keeps the UCLA affiliation from the Atlas paper; update if Petr prefers Altos Labs with a confirmed location. The 2013 date for the Horvath clock is from general knowledge of Genome Biology 2013, not from a page read today.

Parmigiani A.lab_name: Budanov Lab, Department of Human and Molecular Genetics, Virginia Commonwealth University (Richmond, Virginia, USA)
Parmigiani A.role: Molecular biologist who worked in Andrei Budanov's lab at Virginia Commonwealth University on Sestrins, stress-induced proteins that hold back mTORC1
Parmigiani A.sub: Department of Human and Molecular Genetics, Goodwin Research Laboratories, Massey Cancer Center, Virginia Commonwealth University (papers with Andrei Budanov, 2014–2019, at the time of the study)
story: Sestrins are proteins that cells make when they are under stress, for example after DNA damage, and they help switch off mTORC1, the growth-control complex. In PAR2014, Anita Parmigiani and colleagues in Andrei Budanov's lab showed in cultured cells how this works. Sestrins bind to GATOR2, a protein complex that normally helps turn mTORC1 on at the lysosome when amino acids are present. By holding GATOR2 back, Sestrins keep the Rag proteins in their inactive state, so mTORC1 cannot be recruited and switched on. The study helped place Sestrins inside the amino acid sensing pathway that controls mTORC1.

Parmigiani published with the Budanov group at Virginia Commonwealth University from 2014 to 2019, on Sestrins and their links to p53, mTORC1 and mTORC2. In a 2019 study of mouse lung cancer and human lung cancer cells, the group found that losing Sestrin2 sped up early tumour growth through AKT, while Sestrins could also slow later stages when nutrients are scarce. No current institutional page was found, so the affiliation shown is the one on the Atlas paper.

highlights.PAR2014: First author: showed in cultured cells that Sestrins inhibit mTORC1 by acting on the GATOR2 complex.

sources: PubMed search Parmigiani A[Author] AND (Sestrin OR mTOR OR p53), 6 papers 2014-2019

Dąbkowska A.lab_name: Laboratory of Immunology, Mossakowski Medical Research Institute, Polish Academy of Sciences (Warsaw, Poland)
Dąbkowska A.role: Leukemia researcher in Warsaw who works on new drug combinations for B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia, including mTORC1 inhibitors that make leukemia cells easier targets for anti-CD20 antibodies
Dąbkowska A.sub: Laboratory of Immunology, Mossakowski Medical Research Institute, Polish Academy of Sciences · Department of Immunology, Medical University of Warsaw (papers with Malgorzata Firczuk, 2024–2026)
story: B-cell precursor acute lymphoblastic leukemia (BCP-ALL) is the most common childhood cancer. Antibody drugs such as rituximab attack cells that carry the surface protein CD20, but many BCP-ALL cells show little CD20, so the antibodies have few places to grab. In DAB2026, Agnieszka Dąbkowska and colleagues in Malgorzata Firczuk's group found that drugs blocking mTORC1, the growth-control complex, raise CD20 on these leukemia cells. The route runs through AKT and the transcription factor FOXO1, and the treated cells also move a step further along B-cell maturation. As a result, anti-CD20 antibodies killed leukemia cells better, including in high-risk disease with deletions in the IKZF1 gene. The study gives a laboratory rationale for combining mTORC1 inhibitors with CD20-targeted antibodies; it is not a clinical trial.

Dąbkowska works with the Firczuk group at the Mossakowski Medical Research Institute of the Polish Academy of Sciences and the Department of Immunology of the Medical University of Warsaw. In 2024 Dąbkowska was a co-author of a study showing that blocking the antioxidant enzyme peroxiredoxin-1 together with a DNA repair pathway makes Philadelphia-positive B-ALL much more sensitive to tyrosine kinase inhibitors. No personal institutional page was found, so the affiliation shown is the one on the Atlas paper.

highlights.DAB2026: First author: showed that mTORC1 inhibitors raise CD20 on B-cell precursor ALL cells via AKT-FOXO1 and improve the effect of anti-CD20 antibodies.

Dąbkowska A.note: Statement that BCP-ALL is the most common childhood cancer and the rituximab example are general background, not from the paper record.

Firczuk M.lab_name: Laboratory of Immunology, Mossakowski Medical Research Institute, Polish Academy of Sciences (Warsaw, Poland)
Firczuk M.role: Immunologist in Warsaw who leads research on the weak points of B-cell leukemias and lymphomas, from the thioredoxin antioxidant system to combinations of mTORC1 inhibitors with antibody drugs
Firczuk M.sub: Laboratory of Immunology, Mossakowski Medical Research Institute, Polish Academy of Sciences · Department of Immunology, Medical University of Warsaw
story: In DAB2026, Malgorzata Firczuk's group in Warsaw asked whether blocking mTORC1, the growth-control complex, could help antibody drugs that target CD20, a protein on the surface of B cells. In B-cell precursor acute lymphoblastic leukemia, CD20 is often low. The team found that mTORC1 inhibitors raise CD20 through AKT and the transcription factor FOXO1 and push the leukemia cells towards a more mature B-cell state, which made anti-CD20 antibodies work better, including in high-risk disease with IKZF1 deletions. This is preclinical work that supports testing the combination; it does not show benefit in patients.

Firczuk works at the Department of Immunology of the Medical University of Warsaw and the Laboratory of Immunology of the Mossakowski Medical Research Institute, Polish Academy of Sciences, and has about two dozen PubMed papers on leukemia and lymphoma. A recurring theme is how leukemia cells handle oxidative stress. In 2024, as senior author, Firczuk reported that the antioxidant enzyme peroxiredoxin-1 is high in Philadelphia-positive B-ALL, and that blocking the thioredoxin system together with a DNA repair route called non-homologous end joining makes these cells much more sensitive to tyrosine kinase inhibitors such as imatinib.

highlights.DAB2026: Senior author: led the study showing that mTORC1 inhibition raises CD20 and improves anti-CD20 antibody efficacy in B-cell precursor ALL.

sources: PubMed search Firczuk M[Author] AND (leukemia OR lymphoma), 24 results

Zeng H.lab_name: Zeng Lab, Division of Rheumatology, Department of Medicine, and Department of Immunology, Mayo Clinic (Rochester, Minnesota, USA)
Zeng H.role: Immunologist at Mayo Clinic who studies how mTOR signalling and cell metabolism shape T cells in autoimmunity, and who showed as a postdoc that regulatory T cells need mTORC1 to work
Zeng H.sub: Division of Rheumatology, Department of Medicine, and Department of Immunology, Mayo Clinic, Rochester · postdoc, Hongbo Chi lab, Department of Immunology, St. Jude Children's Research Hospital, Memphis (at the time of the study)
story: Regulatory T cells, or Tregs, are the immune system's peacekeepers: they stop other immune cells from attacking the body's own tissues. It had been thought that mTORC1, the growth-control complex, mainly works against Tregs, because rapamycin can help them expand. In ZEN2013, Hu Zeng, working in Hongbo Chi's lab at St. Jude Children's Research Hospital, showed in mice that the opposite is also true. When Raptor, an essential part of mTORC1, was removed only from Tregs, the cells lost their suppressive function and the mice developed severe inflammatory disease. mTORC1 was needed to switch on cholesterol and lipid production in Tregs, which they use to keep up their suppressive programme. The study showed that a single signalling hub can both restrain and support the same cell type, depending on context.

Zeng now runs a research group in the Division of Rheumatology and the Department of Immunology at Mayo Clinic in Rochester, Minnesota. The lab studies T cell metabolism and signalling in autoimmune disease, including, in a 2026 study, the immune profile of inflammatory arthritis caused by cancer immunotherapy drugs, which looked driven mainly by T cells rather than autoantibodies.

highlights.ZEN2013: First author: showed in mice that regulatory T cells lacking mTORC1 lose their suppressive function, linking mTORC1 to Treg lipid metabolism.

sources: PubMed search Zeng H[Author] AND Mayo Clinic[Affiliation] AND (T cell OR mTOR), 19 results

It is not an Atlas paper and is not mentioned in the profile. ZEN2013 details (Raptor deletion, inflammatory disease, cholesterol/lipid synthesis) are from the paper's known abstract, not re-read today. No Mayo profile page could be opened.

Evans S.lab_name: Department of Integrative Neuroscience, Guarini School of Graduate and Advanced Studies, Dartmouth College (Hanover, New Hampshire, USA)
Evans S.role: Neuroscience researcher at Dartmouth who studies how growth signals shape the skeleton of sensory nerve fibres, and first author of work showing that PTEN acts on microtubules through mTORC2 rather than mTORC1
Evans S.sub: Department of Integrative Neuroscience, Guarini School of Graduate and Advanced Studies, Dartmouth College (at the time of the study, 2026)
story: PTEN is a brake on the PI3K growth pathway. When nerve cells lose PTEN, they grow larger and their axons, the long fibres that carry signals, extend faster. Both mTOR complexes sit downstream of PTEN: mTORC1, best known for driving protein synthesis, and mTORC2, which acts more on the cell's internal skeleton. In EVA2026, Simone Evans and colleagues at Dartmouth asked which of the two carries the signal in peripheral sensory neurons. Using mouse genetics, they removed PTEN together with either Raptor, an essential part of mTORC1, or Rictor, an essential part of mTORC1's sister complex mTORC2. Removing mTORC2, but not mTORC1, brought the fast growth of microtubules, the protein tracks inside axons, and the enlarged size of PTEN-deficient neurons back to normal. The effect was seen at the growth cone, the moving tip of the axon, not along the axon shaft. The work adds evidence on the less studied mTORC2 side of the pathway.

Evans is a member of the Department of Integrative Neuroscience at Dartmouth's Guarini School of Graduate and Advanced Studies, the school that runs Dartmouth's PhD programmes. EVA2026 is the only PubMed paper found under this name and affiliation, so no wider research record is described here.

highlights.EVA2026: First author: used Raptor or Rictor co-deletion in PTEN-deficient sensory neurons to show that mTORC2, not mTORC1, drives faster microtubule growth at the axon tip.

Stork B.lab_name: Institute of Molecular Medicine I, Medical Faculty and University Hospital Düsseldorf, Heinrich Heine University (Düsseldorf, North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany)
Stork B.role: Cell biologist in Düsseldorf who studies the ULK1 complex, the switch that starts autophagy, and how it is wired to the energy sensor AMPK and to mTOR
Stork B.sub: Institute of Molecular Medicine I, Heinrich Heine University Düsseldorf (papers 2015–2026) · Department of Internal Medicine I, University of Tübingen (at the time of LOF2011)
story: Autophagy, the cell's self-digestion system, is started by a protein kinase called ULK1. When energy runs low, the energy sensor AMPK switches ULK1 on, and when nutrients are plentiful mTORC1 switches it off. In LOF2011, from Björn Stork's group, then at the University of Tübingen, Antje Löffler and colleagues found that the signal also runs backwards: ULK1 adds phosphate groups to AMPK and dampens its activity. This makes a negative feedback loop, a built-in way for the autophagy machinery to limit the signal that started it, rather than a one-way switch. The work was done in cell and biochemical experiments.

Stork's group later moved to the Institute of Molecular Medicine I at Heinrich Heine University Düsseldorf, where it continued to dissect the ULK1 complex. In 2015 the team mapped the short stretch of the protein ATG13 that holds ULK1 in place and found that cells lacking this contact still keep some autophagy, which points to routes that bypass the usual ULK1-ATG13 link. In 2026, as senior author, Stork reported that human induced pluripotent stem cells and nerve progenitor cells have working autophagy machinery but do not switch it on after low-dose DNA damage, unlike many cancer cell lines.

highlights.LOF2011: Senior author: led the study showing that ULK1 phosphorylates and inhibits AMPK, forming a negative feedback loop in autophagy signalling.

sources: PubMed search Stork B[Author] AND (autophagy OR ULK1) AND Düsseldorf, 33 results
Stork B.note: Position title (e.g. professor, group leader) not confirmed; no official profile page could be opened because the web search budget ran out.

Löffler AS.lab_name: Stork group, Institute of Molecular Medicine I, Heinrich Heine University Düsseldorf (Düsseldorf, North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany)
Löffler AS.role: Cell biologist who worked in Björn Stork's group on how the autophagy kinase ULK1 talks back to the energy sensor AMPK
Löffler AS.sub: Institute of Molecular Medicine I, Heinrich Heine University Düsseldorf (papers to 2015) · Department of Internal Medicine I, University of Tübingen (at the time of LOF2011)
story: In LOF2011, Antje Löffler was first author of the study from Björn Stork's group at the University of Tübingen showing that ULK1, the kinase that starts autophagy, phosphorylates and inhibits AMPK, the energy sensor that normally switches ULK1 on. The result is a negative feedback loop: once autophagy has been triggered, ULK1 turns down the signal that started it. This matters for the mTOR field because AMPK and mTORC1 both act on ULK1 from opposite sides, so a loop back to AMPK changes how the whole system responds to starvation. The work was done in cell and biochemical experiments.

Löffler appears on seven PubMed papers from 2011 to 2015, all on autophagy signalling with Stork and Sebastian Wesselborg, first in Tübingen and then at the Institute of Molecular Medicine I of Heinrich Heine University Düsseldorf. They include a 2015 study mapping the ULK1-binding site on the autophagy protein ATG13. No later papers or institutional page were found, so the affiliation shown is the last one on these papers.

highlights.LOF2011: First author: showed that ULK1 phosphorylates AMPK and inhibits it, a negative feedback loop in autophagy signalling.

Rauch B.lab_name: Bai Lab, Department of Medical Chemistry, Faculty of Medicine, University of Debrecen (Debrecen, Hungary)
Rauch B.role: Researcher in Péter Bai's group at the University of Debrecen who studies how ADP-ribosylating enzymes control fat cell development through AMPK and mTOR
Rauch B.sub: Department of Medical Chemistry, Faculty of Medicine, University of Debrecen (papers 2019–2026)
story: Fat cells form from precursor cells in a process called adipocyte differentiation, which needs mTORC1, the growth-control complex, to be active. In RAUCH2026, Boglarka Rauch and colleagues in Péter Bai's group worked on tankyrases, enzymes that attach chains of ADP-ribose to other proteins and so change how those proteins behave. In a cell line, deleting tankyrase-1 or tankyrase-2 slowed fat cell formation. The cells showed active AMPK, the energy sensor, low mTORC1 activity and blocked autophagy. The defect caused by losing tankyrase-2 could be fixed by NV-5138, a drug that switches mTORC1 on, or by blocking LKB1, the kinase that activates AMPK. Tankyrase-2 was found to ADP-ribosylate LKB1, which suggests that it normally keeps the LKB1-AMPK brake on mTORC1 in check. The findings come from cultured cells only.

Rauch has published with the Bai group in the Department of Medical Chemistry at the University of Debrecen since 2019, including a 2023 screen of bacterial metabolites for effects on breast cancer cell growth. No personal institutional page was found, so the affiliation shown is the one on the Atlas paper.

highlights.RAUCH2026: First author: showed in a cell line that tankyrase-2 supports fat cell differentiation through the LKB1-AMPK-mTORC1 axis and ADP-ribosylates LKB1.

sources: PubMed search Rauch B[Author] AND Debrecen, 6 results 2019-2026

Berger Z.lab_name: Rubinsztein Lab, Cambridge Institute for Medical Research, University of Cambridge (Cambridge, England, United Kingdom)
Berger Z.role: Neuroscientist who, in David Rubinsztein's lab in Cambridge, showed that rapamycin-induced autophagy lowers the toxicity of several disease proteins that form clumps, including tau in fruit flies
Berger Z.sub: Department of Medical Genetics, Cambridge Institute for Medical Research, Addenbrooke's Hospital, University of Cambridge (at the time of the study, 2006)
story: Several brain diseases, including Huntington's disease and some dementias, are caused by proteins that misfold and clump together. Autophagy, the cell's self-cleaning system, can remove such clumps, and rapamycin switches autophagy on by blocking mTOR. In BER2006, Zdenek Berger, working in David Rubinsztein's lab in Cambridge, extended the group's earlier huntingtin work. In cultured cells, rapamycin increased the clearance of several proteins with long stretches of the amino acid glutamine, and of a protein with an extended alanine stretch, and reduced their toxicity. In fruit flies carrying normal or mutant human tau, rapamycin lowered tau toxicity and the amount of insoluble tau. The authors proposed that inducing autophagy might help in a range of clumping-protein diseases. The evidence comes from cells and flies only, with no data in mammals or people.

PubMed lists about 14 papers under this name on huntingtin, tau, LRRK2 and alpha-synuclein, the proteins behind Huntington's, Alzheimer's and Parkinson's diseases. No current institutional page was found, so the affiliation shown is the one on the Atlas paper.

highlights.BER2006: First author: showed that rapamycin speeds the clearance and lowers the toxicity of several aggregate-prone proteins in cells, and of tau in flies.

Menzies FM.lab_name: Rubinsztein Lab, Cambridge Institute for Medical Research, University of Cambridge (Cambridge, England, United Kingdom)
Menzies FM.role: Cell biologist who worked for many years in David Rubinsztein's Cambridge lab on autophagy and the clearance of disease proteins in neurodegeneration
Menzies FM.sub: Department of Medical Genetics, Cambridge Institute for Medical Research, University of Cambridge School of Clinical Medicine (papers with David Rubinsztein, 2006–2021)
story: Fiona Menzies is a co-author on two Atlas papers from David Rubinsztein's lab. BER2006 showed in cultured cells that rapamycin, by switching on autophagy, the cell's self-cleaning system, helps clear several clumping proteins linked to brain disease and reduces their toxicity, and that it lowers toxicity of human tau in fruit flies. KOR2011 found that where the lysosome sits in the cell helps decide whether mTORC1, the growth-control complex, is on: with nutrients present lysosomes move to the cell edge and mTORC1 is active, while starvation pulls them towards the nucleus, mTORC1 falls and autophagy starts.

PubMed lists more than 40 papers that Menzies co-authored with Rubinsztein, from the mid-2000s to 2021, many on autophagy in neurodegenerative disease and on ways to raise autophagy with drugs or genetic tools. No current institutional page was found, so the affiliation shown is the one on the Atlas papers.

highlights.KOR2011: Co-author on the paper showing that lysosome position inside the cell tunes mTORC1 activity and autophagy.

Majumder PK.lab_name: Sellers Lab, Department of Medical Oncology, Dana-Farber Cancer Institute (Boston, Massachusetts, USA)
Majumder PK.role: Cancer biologist who, in William Sellers's lab at Dana-Farber, showed that mTOR inhibitors reverse AKT-driven early prostate cancer in mice
Majumder PK.sub: Department of Medical Oncology, Dana-Farber Cancer Institute, and Department of Medicine, Brigham and Women's Hospital, Harvard Medical School (at the time of the study, 2004)
story: AKT is a growth kinase that is often overactive in prostate cancer, usually because the brake PTEN is lost. In MAJ2004, Pradip Majumder and colleagues in William Sellers's lab used mice that make active AKT in the prostate. These mice develop prostatic intraepithelial neoplasia (PIN), an early, pre-invasive stage of prostate cancer. Treating them with the mTOR inhibitor RAD001 (everolimus) reversed the PIN. The authors traced the effect to two routes: the drug caused the abnormal cells to die by apoptosis, and it switched off a set of genes controlled by HIF-1, a transcription factor that drives growth and blood vessel formation. The study, done in mice, helped make the case that tumours driven by AKT depend on mTOR and could respond to mTOR inhibitors.
No current institutional page was found. The affiliation shown is the one on the Atlas paper.

highlights.MAJ2004: First author: showed in AKT-transgenic mice that the mTOR inhibitor RAD001 reverses prostatic intraepithelial neoplasia through apoptosis and HIF-1-dependent pathways.

Wagle N.lab_name: Department of Medical Oncology, Dana-Farber Cancer Institute (Boston, Massachusetts, USA)
Wagle N.role: Medical oncologist and cancer genomics researcher at Dana-Farber who studies why some patients respond exceptionally well to targeted drugs, including a patient whose tumour carried two activating MTOR mutations
Wagle N.sub: Department of Medical Oncology and Center for Molecular Oncologic Pathology, Dana-Farber Cancer Institute; Brigham and Women's Hospital, Harvard Medical School (at the time of the study, 2014)
story: Most patients in early drug trials see little benefit, but now and then one patient responds far better than anyone else. Studying these 'exceptional responders' can reveal what makes a tumour sensitive. In WAG2014, Nikhil Wagle and colleagues sequenced the tumour of a patient who had an extraordinary response on a phase I trial of everolimus, an mTOR inhibitor, combined with pazopanib. The tumour carried two activating mutations in the MTOR gene itself at the same time, which made it dependent on mTOR and so vulnerable to everolimus. Because it is a single patient, the finding generates a hypothesis; it does not show that MTOR mutations predict response in general.

At the time of the study Wagle worked in the Department of Medical Oncology and the Center for Molecular Oncologic Pathology at Dana-Farber Cancer Institute and at Brigham and Women's Hospital, Harvard Medical School. An official current profile could not be opened for this batch, so later positions are not described here.

highlights.WAG2014: First author: found two concurrent activating MTOR mutations in the tumour of a patient with an exceptional response to everolimus plus pazopanib.

Hudes G.lab_name: Department of Medical Oncology, Fox Chase Cancer Center (Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, USA)
Hudes G.role: Medical oncologist at Fox Chase Cancer Center who led the phase 3 trial showing that the mTOR inhibitor temsirolimus lengthens survival in poor-prognosis advanced kidney cancer
Hudes G.sub: Department of Medical Oncology, Fox Chase Cancer Center, Philadelphia (at the time of the study, 2007)
story: In HUD2007, Gary Hudes was first author of the large randomised trial of temsirolimus, one of the first mTOR inhibitors tested in cancer. Patients with advanced kidney cancer and a poor outlook were given temsirolimus, interferon alfa (the standard treatment of the time), or both. Temsirolimus alone extended median overall survival to 10.9 months, compared with 7.3 months on interferon alfa. Rash, high blood sugar and high blood fats were more common with temsirolimus, which fits with mTOR's role in controlling metabolism. The trial is one of the strongest human data sets in this Atlas because it is a randomised phase 3 study.

At the time of the trial Hudes worked in the Department of Medical Oncology at Fox Chase Cancer Center in Philadelphia. The PubMed record under 'Hudes G' and 'Hudes GR' runs to more than 170 papers, but the name matches other authors as well, so the later career is not described here.

highlights.HUD2007: First author: reported the phase 3 trial in which temsirolimus alone gave longer survival than interferon alfa in poor-prognosis advanced kidney cancer.

Walter T.lab_name: Department of Medical Oncology, Hôpital Édouard Herriot, Hospices Civils de Lyon (Lyon, France)
Walter T.role: Medical oncologist in Lyon who specialises in neuroendocrine tumours and led the COMPETE phase 3 trial comparing 177Lu-edotreotide with everolimus
Walter T.sub: Department of Medical Oncology, Hôpital Édouard Herriot, Lyon (at the time of the study, 2026)
story: Neuroendocrine tumours of the gut and pancreas grow from hormone-making cells. Many carry receptors for the hormone somatostatin on their surface, which can be used to deliver radiation straight to the tumour: a somatostatin-like molecule is linked to a radioactive atom such as lutetium-177, an approach called peptide receptor radionuclide therapy. Everolimus, an mTOR inhibitor, is a standard drug for these tumours. In WALTER2026, Thomas Walter was first author of COMPETE, a phase 3 randomised trial in 309 patients that compared 177Lu-edotreotide with everolimus. Median progression-free survival was 23.9 months with the radioligand and 14.1 months with everolimus, and serious treatment-related side effects were less common (18 percent against 40 percent). The trial was open-label, so patients and doctors knew which treatment was given. For the mTOR field, the result means an mTOR inhibitor was the comparator that a newer therapy beat in this disease.
Walter works in the Department of Medical Oncology at Hôpital Édouard Herriot in Lyon. PubMed lists more than 140 papers under this name on neuroendocrine tumours with Lyon affiliations.

highlights.WALTER2026: First author: reported the COMPETE trial, in which 177Lu-edotreotide gave longer progression-free survival than everolimus with fewer severe side effects.
